body: Early on, working in agencies, I kept seeing the same problem: designers who didn't understand how their work would be built, developers who'd let basic design fundamentals stay mysterious, and teams somehow having more meetings without understanding each other any better.

I got a little obsessed with that problem. I'd seen companies pair programmers, and it felt natural that design, development, and product should work that closely too. I tried integrating those workflows into the teams I was on, but it's hard to change habits once everyone's settled into their corner. Eventually I thought: there should be a school that teaches the whole thing together from the beginning.

So I built one. I designed the curriculum, programmed the platform, built the business and the systems behind it, and spent years working through real problems with hundreds of designers and developers. The thesis was pretty simple: the work gets better when we're one team instead of "designers" and "coders" handing things back and forth.

I kept doing product work in parallel. One project was a green-field real estate platform where the forms, legal machinery, seller education, messaging, and actual product all had to be figured out together. Another brought a bunch of disconnected financial education tools into one coherent product. Different problems, same basic job: figure out what we're really trying to do, then make all the pieces agree.

That's the kind of product design I like. I can research the problem, work through the IA and flows, design the interface, prototype in code, and stay with it long enough to find out whether any of our assumptions were right. We can always flip through Mobbin and find some nice UI flourishes. The bigger system is the interesting part.

I've spent about 15 years learning how to do the whole thing. I don't need to be the person doing every part. I like knowing enough about all the parts that we can figure things out together. Give me the messy problem, the people who understand different pieces of it, a whiteboard, Figma, some code... whatever gets us somewhere. I want to be on a team where we're making each other better.
I've spent most of my career being the person who can make the design and also figure out how it's actually going to work.

Sometimes that meant building a weird interactive thing for a campaign that only needed to live for a few weeks. Other times it meant designing something that had to become a real system and survive years of new features, new people, and changing requirements. Doing both taught me when to move fast, when to slow down, and which decisions you're going to regret pretending don't matter.

Eventually I got interested enough in that overlap to build a school around it. At Perpetual Education, I taught designers how the web actually works and developers how typography, hierarchy, interaction, and visual systems work. Teaching it over and over also gave me a ridiculous amount of time to test my own ideas about how design and engineering should fit together.

I'm usually thinking about the stuff between the mockup and the component: naming, states, tokens, typography, responsive behavior, theming, scope, what belongs in the system and what's really just a one-off.

But really, you can hand me a drawing on a napkin. We can figure out the routes, get the CSS foundation in place, establish the tokens and components, and then get everybody in there pushing it around. I don't care whose idea wins. I care that we can actually try the ideas and find out.

I've worked across design and development for about 15 years. I know enough about both sides to know that neither one has all the answers. Pull me into the weird meeting. Show me the thing that's driving everybody nuts. Let's make something we can poke at instead of arguing about it. That's the space I want to work in, with people who are really good at what they do.

I learned to build for the web by digging through Stack Overflow threads, documentation, blog posts, and whatever else I could find. Sometimes I'd lose half a day trying to understand something, finally get it working, and realize... wait, that's it?
That happened enough times that I got really interested in why some explanations work and others don't.

Eventually I started helping other people through the same things. That turned into mentoring, then workshops, and eventually Perpetual Education, the design and programming school I built and ran for seven years. I've now watched hundreds of designers and developers get stuck in just about every way imaginable.

I love it. That moment when somebody's mental model changes and the thing that seemed impossible five minutes ago suddenly feels obvious? That's fun. And I've learned that it's rarely about just giving somebody the answer. It's about setting up the situation where the learning can actually happen.

I'm a lifelong learner and still a product designer and developer. So whether the job is writing docs, interviewing users, designing an example project, making a tutorial, kicking the tires on a new product, doing some weird R&D, running a workshop, or figuring out why everybody keeps getting stuck on the same feature: I'm here for it.

I don't really think of advocacy as explaining features. I want to learn the thing with people. Kick the tires, find the weird edges, figure out where people are getting lost, help them get really good at it, and bring everything we learn back to the people building it.
That sounds like a pretty great job to me.
